nameStory: The Green-tailed Towhee gets its name from the bright green stripes along the edges of its wings, which flash like little emerald banners when it flies. The word 'towhee' comes from the call of its eastern cousin, though this western bird has its own distinctive voice that sounds more like a cat's mew than the classic 'tow-hee' call.
description: The Green-tailed Towhee is a striking medium-sized songbird that's the smallest member of the towhee family, yet still larger than most sparrows. Picture a bird about the size of a robin but built more compactly, with a bright rusty-red cap, clean white throat, and those distinctive green wing stripes that give it its name. At about 7 inches long, it's a beautiful bird that prefers to stay hidden in dense brush, making it a special treat when you do spot one. Despite being primarily a western bird, a few adventurous individuals occasionally show up in New England as rare visitors.

idTips.label: Green wing stripes
idTips.description: Look for bright green or olive-green stripes along the wing edges that flash when the bird moves or flies - no other New England bird has this distinctive green wing pattern

idTips.label: Rusty cap and white throat
idTips.description: Sports a bright reddish-brown or rufous cap on top of its head paired with a clean, bright white throat that looks almost like it's wearing a white bib

idTips.label: Secretive behavior
idTips.description: Tends to stay hidden deep in dense bushes and thickets, often heard scratching through leaf litter like a tiny chicken before you see it

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Noticeably larger and more robust than typical sparrows, with a thick, seed-cracking bill and sturdy legs built for ground foraging

idTips.label: Call and sounds
idTips.description: Makes a distinctive cat-like 'mew' call and produces a sweet, varied song with trills and whistles when it does vocalize

habitat: In New England, this rare visitor would most likely be found in dense shrublands, overgrown fields, or woodland edges with thick understory vegetation. Look for areas with dense brush piles, brambles, or young forest growth where the bird can forage on the ground while staying well-hidden. Since it prefers sagebrush habitat in its western range, it might also turn up in scrubby areas or abandoned lots with similar dense, low vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare during spring migration, but any sightings would likely occur in dense brush where the bird would be actively foraging and possibly singing its sweet, complex song.
seasonality.summer: Not expected during summer months in New England, as this species breeds in the interior western United States and would not be found in our region during breeding season.
seasonality.fall: The most likely time to spot this rare visitor during fall migration, when it might turn up at bird feeders or in dense shrublands while seeking shelter and food.
seasonality.winter: Occasionally reported at winter bird feeders, especially during harsh weather when it seeks reliable food sources, though still extremely uncommon in New England.

funFact: Despite being called a sparrow family member, Green-tailed Towhees are actually more closely related to cardinals and tanagers than to Old World sparrows - they're part of a uniquely American bird family that evolved separately on this continent!
confusionNotes: The green wing stripes and rusty cap make this bird quite distinctive, but a quick glimpse might confuse it with a large sparrow. However, no other New England bird combines the green wings with the bright white throat and rufous cap - if you see those green wing stripes, you've found something very special indeed!
contextualKnowledge: The Green-tailed Towhee is classified as a 'New World Sparrow' in the family Passerellidae, which despite the name, are not actually true sparrows but rather a uniquely American group of seed-eating songbirds. This family split from the Old World sparrows millions of years ago and evolved independently in the Americas.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin the Eastern Towhee which is boldly patterned in black, white, and rufous with no green coloring, the Green-tailed Towhee is much smaller and more subtly colored overall. While Eastern Towhees are common year-round residents with striking black heads and backs, Green-tailed Towhees are rare visitors with olive-gray bodies and those unmistakable green wing stripes. The Eastern Towhee also gives the classic 'drink-your-tea' call, while the Green-tailed makes softer mewing sounds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern Towhees are the only Pipilo towhee species in New England - their closest relatives are the Spotted Towhee of the west (which has white spots on the back instead of solid coloring) and the Green-tailed Towhee (which is greenish with a rusty cap).
Spotted Towhees differ from their close relative the Eastern Towhee primarily by those diagnostic white spots on wings and back - Eastern Towhees lack these spots entirely.
